taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes that Virginia is polyphyletic (Haldea resurrected for V. striatula) and that V. valeriae is close to Tropidoclonion lineatum; no source read renames V. valeriae itself.
fieldMarks: Small snake 6-13 in; gray, tan, brown or red-brown above with tiny black dots on the head and a faint pale line down the back in some.
Pale yellow to white below; scales smooth or weakly keeled in 17 rows.
Compared with the rough earth snake it has 6 upper-lip scales, 2 scales between the nostrils and 2 postoculars, and an always-divided anal plate (Missouri Department of Conservation comparison).
behavior: Secretive; hides in leaf litter, pulpy logs or under logs and trash; may aggregate in hibernation.
Eats mainly earthworms, also slugs and small soft-bodied invertebrates; gives birth to 3-8 young.
Active April to October/November in the north; surface activity peaks after heavy rains.
habitat: Deciduous and pine woods, rocky wooded slopes, moist floodplain woodland, forest edges, old fields and wooded residential areas.
range: Eastern and central United States: Alabama, Arkansas, Delaware, DC, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia and West Virginia; not in Canada.
